Static Voltage Stability Criterion of Renewable
Energy Sources based on Power Flow Analysis
Mengke Lu
State Grid Zhejiang Electric Power Company
Hangzhou, China

Zhoushan, China
18768053583@163.com

Jinan, China

Abstract—With the continuous increase in the penetration rate
of new energy sources, the strength of the power grid gradually
weakens, and the anti-interference capability of the system also
decreases accordingly. Therefore, the real-time identification of
the static voltage stability of power systems is of particular
importance. The traditional approach for identifying the static
voltage stability boundary of power systems is the P-V curve
method. However, this method exhibits high computational
complexity and strong dependence on the operational scenarios of
the system, making it difficult to meet the requirements of real-
time monitoring under complex scenarios. In view of this, this
paper proposes a static voltage stability assessment method based
on the singular points of the Jacobian matrix, and theoretically
proves the effectiveness of this novel voltage stability assessment
method. The reliability of the proposed method is verified through
simulations.
Keywords—Grid-following converter, Control strategy, Static
voltage stability, Jacobian matrix.
I. I NTRODUCTION
With the continuous increase in the penetration rate of
renewable energy source (RES), the number of voltage source
converters (VSC) connected to the power grid has been
increasing progressively, which leads to a gradual weakening of
grid strength[1]-[3]. Concurrently, the system's capability to
resist disturbances decreases accordingly, and the interaction
between inverters and the AC power grid may give rise to
unstable fluctuations in grid voltage [4]. To accurately evaluate
system fluctuations, proactively identify the risks of static
voltage instability, and optimize power grid structure as well as
equipment configuration, the assessment of static voltage
stability assumes crucial significance.
At present, two primary methods are widely applied to the
calculation of static voltage stability in power systems: the P-V
curve method [5]-[6] and the Q-V curve method [7]-[8]. The
former can intuitively reflect the stability margin but requires a
large number of power flow calculations. The latter, on the
other hand, can clearly demonstrate the robustness of node
voltage to reactive power but only one node can be considered
at a tim. Therefore, both of the aforementioned methods have
limitations in engineering applications.
This paper proposes a novel method for determining the
static voltage stability of power systems by analyzing the
singular points of the Jacobian matrix of power flow equations.
Unlike the traditional P-V curve method, which relies on
complex continuous power flow iterative calculations, this
method directly solves the critical voltage amplitude using the
line impedance modulus and the new energy output power
modulus. This significantly simplifies the calculation process of
critical voltage and enhances the capability of rapid
identification of the static voltage stability boundary.

The present invention uses this method to replace the
consideration of P-V curve (nose curve) with the consideration
of the power circle of Jacobian matrix singular points. Avoiding
the problem of complex calculations for continuous power flow
in P-V curves and simplifying the assessment of system static
voltage stability.
Compared with the PV curve method, this proposed method
can significantly reduce the computation time. For a simplified
system with a single line, the single computation time of this
method ranges from 10 nanoseconds to 5 microseconds,
whereas the single computation time of the PV curve method
(per Pk) is between 50 and 100 microseconds, representing a
time reduction of approximately 98.7%.For complex systems
with multiple nodes and multiple lines, the simplified criterion
is extended to the "comprehensive criterion for multi-line
systems" (e.g., the criterion value is calculated for each line, and
the minimum value is adopted as the system stability index).
Assuming there are 10 lines, the single computation time of the
extended simplified criterion method is 100 nanoseconds to 50
microseconds, while that of thePV curve method is 500 to 1000
microseconds, corresponding to a time reduction of about
93.3%.In conclusion, whether for a simplified single-line
system or a complex multi-node system, the power flow
calculation method based on the simplified criterion proposed
in this paper demonstrates disruptive advantages in
computation time compared with the traditional PV curve
method.

As can be seen, with other parameters unchanged, as the
active output of the new energy grid connected system
increases, the system terminal voltage U gradually decreases
until it collapses. In the case of TABLE 2, criterion Χ  is
approximately close to the grid voltage E=1, which can be used
as a critical stability condition. When criterion > EΧ , the
static voltage of the output system is stable. When criterion
< EΧ , the static voltage of the output system is unstable. Note
again that this example is for load, weakPQ is for power supply,
and attention should be paid to the flow direction of P and Q.
Mechanism of terminal voltage collapse: The continuous
increase in active output of the output system leads to an
increase in line current, and the reactive power loss of the line
is proportional to the square of the current. However, the lack
of reactive power support in the new energy grid connected
system leads to a decrease in terminal voltage, which in turn
requires a larger current to transmit the same active power,
triggering a vicious cycle and ultimately forming voltage
collapse, as shown in Fig. 6. When the voltage U is less than
0.9E, the criterion for voltage stability should be applied. When

becomes unstable. Combining the trend of the curve: 2 seconds

was running normally, and the active output of the new energy
grid connected system continued to increase. At this point,

When the Q is increased to 0.6 p.u., it is observed that the
system voltage collapse time is delayed by approximately 0.55
seconds, and the system’s static voltage stability margin is
significantly enhanced. The additional reactive power reserve
can effectively offset the line voltage drop effect caused by the
increase in P, thereby delaying the cascading process of static
voltage instability. Ultimately, this manifests as a notable delay
in the time interval from when the system approaches the
stability limit to when voltage collapse occurs.
Considering the scenario where multiple renewable energy
stations are connected to the grid, it is assumed that the
parameters of VSC1 remain as presented in Table 1. VSC2 is
connected in parallel with VSC1, and all parameters of VSC2
are identical to those of VSC1, except that its active power
reference ( Pref) is increased to 1. This setup is intended to
simulate a fault occurring in VSC1 under the condition of two
parallel-connected VSC stations. The objective of this study is
to verify whether the stability criterion based on Criterion ∆
remains applicable, and the simulation results are presented in
Fig. 7.
In comparison between Fig. 6 and Fig. 8, the values of both
Criterion ∆ and terminal voltage are nearly identical between
the two scenarios. This indicates that under the condition of two
parallel-connected VSC stations, when a fault occurs in one of
the VSC stations, the proposed stability criterion remains
accurate. Therefore, this criterion is applicable to multi-VSC
parallel operation scenarios.

V. C ONCLUSION
By analyzing the singular points of the Jacobian matrix
determinant corresponding to the new energy grid-connected
system, this study proposes a Voltage-Source-Converter -based
voltage stability assessment method. This method eliminates
the reliance of traditional P-V curve methods on continuous
power flow calculations, which demand iterative solving of
modified power flow equations. It simplifies the identification
process of the static voltage stability boundary, improves
computational efficiency, and enhances applicability in
complex operating environments featuring fluctuations and
intermittency of new energy output.
